text:
Random history cropping has clear precedents: [CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14395) samples contiguous subsequences, alongside masking and reordering, to construct contrastive views while retaining a next-item objective. Thus cropping alone offers limited novelty; applying it to supervised all-position NextItNet training requires a more specific claim. [NextItNet’s official implementation](https://github.com/fajieyuan/WSDM2019-nextitnet) also discusses subsequence construction and differences in training-example counts. [DuoRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05730) highlights semantic inconsistency from data-level augmentation, using dropout views and same-target positive sequences instead. [EC4SRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01347) similarly motivates importance-guided augmentation because random transformations need not preserve sequence semantics.

Experimental implication—proposed controls, not established findings: compare full-history training, cropped-history training, and full-history training with exactly the cropped condition’s target-position loss mask. Match sampled users, target identities, negatives, optimizer steps, and loss normalization; the latter pair isolates context removal from reduced or redistributed supervision. Separately compare all-position versus final-position loss under identical contexts. For target-preserving crops, remove only older context while retaining the immediate predecessor; cropping the recent endpoint while retaining the original target changes the prediction horizon. Keep causal masking and prevent targets entering their own inputs. Evaluate every condition with the same prescribed full-history inference and final nonpadding readout. Report retained context lengths and supervised-target counts: an improvement otherwise could reflect target reweighting, altered horizons, or regularization rather than better tolerance of training–inference context mismatch.
